SHMtrace: complete manuscript with supplemental information
SHMtrace calls somatic hypermutation and other AID-driven mutation with a measured false-discovery rate
Abdulmateen Aderinto^{1,3}, Philip Barbulescu^{1,4} and Alberto Martin^{1,2,*}
^{1}Department of Immunology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 1A8, Canada
^{4}Present address: Structural Genomics Consortium, Toronto, ON M5G 1L7, Canada

Somatic hypermutation (SHM) is measured accurately but at low throughput by cloned-amplicon Sanger sequencing, while existing software targets B-cell receptor repertoires. We developed SHMtrace to quantify substitutions and indels against background measured in matched activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)-deficient controls and compare profiles across biological replicates. A Sanger workflow quantifies substitutions and reports control-derived background separately. Evaluation included planted mutations (false-discovery proportions 0.050 and 0.045), simulated lineages, and twelve loci from eleven laboratories across four platforms. Across five nanopore assays, SHMtrace reduced substitution calls in AID-null controls by 64–90% relative to an uncorrected rule from a general-purpose sequence-analysis platform not tuned for SHM. In four assays, AID-active and AID-null libraries separated 66–141-fold in unique-variant density under the zero-call convention. Nanopore reads preserved linkage and gave spectra similar to Sanger in the same mice. Datasets covered engineered diversification and class-switch junctions. SHMtrace provides a reproducible framework for control-informed analysis of AID-associated diversification.

Somatic hypermutation (SHM) diversifies immunoglobulin (Ig) genes in germinal-center B cells. It is initiated by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), which deaminates cytosines in Ig DNA. Replication over the resulting uracils, together with uracil excision and mismatch repair, generates substitutions at G:C and A:T base pairs[@muramatsu2000,@dinoia2007,@methot2017]. Because each repair pathway leaves its own footprint, the frequency, position and spectrum of mutations are key readouts of AID activity and broader lesion processing[@dinoia2002,@rada2004,@rada2002,@zeng2001]. Relatedly, the mouse J_{H}4 downstream intron is widely used as a genomic reporter because it undergoes SHM without directly contributing to antigen binding[@jolly1997,@lebecque1990].

AID activity read out from J_{H}4 amplicons can be measured on various sequencing platforms, each reporting a different kind of evidence. Cloned-amplicon Sanger sequencing reads one molecule at a time at high per-base confidence, though it yields only tens of sequences per animal[@sible2021]. Short reads typical of Illumina sequencers give depth but may not span the complete region[@martin2023]. Long reads from ONT and PacBio span the J_{H}4, so mutations stay linked across the amplicon, and nanopore accuracy now reaches modal values above 99% with R10.4.1 flow cells[@zhang2023,@sereika2022,@sanderson2024]; nanopore sequencing has also been used to sequence Ig genes, where consensus sequencing can absorb errors[@minervini2021,@subassatish2022]. All platforms, however, share the need to separate AID-driven mutation from their own error. A wild-type J_{H}4 intron carries roughly one mutation per 100 bases, whereas the residual error of a single filtered read, especially with nanopore, is within one or two orders of magnitude of that rate and is concentrated at particular positions and sequence contexts[@delahaye2021].

Two common analysis practices make this problem worse. First, general-purpose low-frequency variant callers judge each base by its own quality score[@wilm2012], and the simple rules used in commercial software test candidates one at a time without correcting for the number of tests[@kearse2012]. In the configurations evaluated, neither measures the errors a particular library makes, so mismatches recurring at one position, from PCR, sequence context or a co-amplified paralog, can be counted as SHM mutations. Second, treating reads from the same animal as independent replicates overstates statistical certainty because multiple reads can derive from the same B-cell clone or PCR-amplified molecule[@lazic2010]. Matched AID-null libraries address technical background, whereas group comparisons must account for biological replication by using one summary value per animal. SHM software has instead followed B-cell receptor repertoire sequencing, summarising mutations already identified[@maccarthy2009,@gupta2015,@yaari2013] rather than using matched AID-null controls to separate candidate variants from technical background.

Here we describe SHMtrace, which integrates variant calling calibrated against matched AID-null controls from the same sequencing run with mutation profiling and group comparisons across independent biological replicates, from delivered reads or Sanger chromatograms. We validated it with planted mutations, simulated lineages, twelve loci from eleven laboratories across four platforms, Sanger sequencing of the same mice, and deposited clones from three published Sanger studies, and compared it against LoFreq[@wilm2012], the long-read somatic callers ClairS[@zheng2026] and DeepSomatic[@park2026], the germline callers Clair3[@zheng2022] and DeepVariant[@poplin2018], and the uncorrected Geneious test[@kearse2012].
SHMtrace calibrates substitutions against AID-null controls

SHMtrace starts from the files that a sequencing provider or core facility returns (Figures 1, S1 and S2). Nanopore and Illumina reads are first filtered by length and expected error[@edgar2015] and then aligned with minimap2[@li2018] against the target together with competing references. Sanger chromatograms, by contrast, are assigned to animals through a sample sheet and trimmed to their high-quality core, and UMI-tagged reads can be collapsed to one consensus per molecule (STAR Methods).

The central step is the variant test (Figures 1A and 1C). For each substitution type, strand and base quality, SHMtrace measures how often the AID-null libraries of the same run show that change, and then asks whether a candidate is supported by more reads than this background explains. Because quality scores overstate certainty at the highest qualities (Figure S3), the control rates are multiplied by a margin chosen by leaving one control out at a time. The held-out controls then serve as decoys, in an approach inspired by target–decoy analysis[@elias2007], and SHMtrace keeps the most permissive cutoff at which estimated false calls are at most 5% of calls. This is an empirical estimate rather than a guarantee, since it relies on a few controls representing the samples' background. Finally, alleles carried by at least half the reads are set aside as likely germline or parental differences; because a mutation shared by a dominant lineage can cross the same threshold, this is a heuristic, and every excluded site is reported.

Because it weighs read support against measured background, the read-library test can retain a candidate supported by a single read; repeated sequencing of the same original molecule is not required. Sanger clones instead take a separate counting route (Figure 1C): every substitution at base quality ≥ 20 is counted, and the AID-null clones' mismatch rate gives the expected background, reported beside the counts rather than subtracted. The germline filter, window, automatic checks and animal-level comparisons are shared. The Sanger results below therefore test trace reading, counting, bookkeeping and group comparisons, not the control-calibrated test.

Two C-to-T candidates in an external wild-type Sμ library (WT3) illustrate how matched controls separate mutations from recurrent background (Figure 2). Both had support on both strands and similar base qualities. However, no control supported the substitution at position 165, within a WRC hotspot, at Q≥20, whereas the substitution at position 97 recurred in the controls. SHMtrace therefore retained position 165 (p = 5 × 10^{−19}) and rejected position 97 (p = 1). Across WT3, 88 of 743 candidates met the threshold (p ≤ 0.009).

Downstream, SHMtrace compares groups using one summary value per biological replicate, with Welch tests on log-transformed rates, bootstrapped negative-binomial tests and permutation tests (Figure 1D). It also describes spectra, hotspot use, S5F targeting[@yaari2013] and clustering, estimates uncalled single-read mutations in aggregate, groups reads into junction-defined clones and reconstructs read-level trees (Figure S4).
Planted mutations and simulated lineages quantify recall and false calls

We planted 60 AID-weighted substitutions into each held-out control library, preserving base qualities and assigning 1–20 supporting reads per site, with three repetitions per control (Figure 3). On J_{H}4, SHMtrace recalled 81% overall and 95% among events supported by at least three reads, with 2.6 false calls per library (observed false-discovery proportion, FDP, 0.050). In contrast, Geneious recalled more single-read mutations (60% versus 31%) but produced 4.9 false calls per library (FDP 0.083). Default LoFreq recalled none; disabling its short-read-oriented base-alignment quality correction yielded 34% recall, restricted to mutations with at least five supporting reads. Permissive settings increased recall to 56% with 4.4 false calls per library (Figures 3A and 3D).

We also gave the long-read somatic callers ClairS[@zheng2026] and DeepSomatic[@park2026] the other AID-null libraries as matched normals. Neither recovered planted mutations at default settings, and even with permissive settings ClairS recovered none of 2,160 substitutions, while DeepSomatic recalled 19%, 18%, 5% and 3% on J_{H}4, N114 V_{H}, Sμ and *Pim1*, respectively. Their recall improved at higher allele fractions (Figure 3C), but real SHM mostly lies below that range: 53% of 1,197 retained SHMtrace calls occurred in <1% of reads (Figures 2E and 3C). The germline callers Clair3 and DeepVariant recovered none, consistent with their intended use (Table S1).

On N114 V_{H}, SHMtrace recalled 90% of planted substitutions, including 58% supported by one read, with 2.6 false calls per library (FDP 0.045; Figure 3B). Here Geneious performed similarly, recalling 88% with 2.8 false calls (FDP 0.050), whereas LoFreq without base-alignment quality recalled 34%. On external Sμ and *Pim1* controls at 2,000 reads, SHMtrace recalled 63% and 72% at FDP 0.055 and 0.035, compared with 59% and 64% for Geneious at FDP 0.114 and 0.050; LoFreq recalled 0–26%, with permissive FDP 0.27–0.52 (Figure 3D). To isolate what the controls contribute, two ablations used the same libraries. Without controls, a read-quality test made 5.7–46.6 false calls per library; testing each site against its control error rate instead made 1.3–2.8, but recalled only 27–64%, against SHMtrace's 63–90% (Table S1). Measured background therefore removes most false calls, and the calibrated test recovers the sensitivity a simple per-site comparison loses.

We then called the same libraries at targets from 1% to 30% to test whether the threshold delivers the rate it targets. At the default 5%, the pooled false-discovery proportion was 3.5–5.5% across the four loci, and looser targets stayed at or below their stated rate except J_{H}4 at 10% (13.8%) (Figure S5A). Targets below 5%, however, did not deliver their stated rate on J_{H}4, Sμ or *Pim1* (2.0–6.1% at a 1% target; N114 V_{H}, 0.5%): false calls per library levelled off while recall fell, from 81% to 17% on J_{H}4 (Figures S5B and S5C).

Because everything rests on the controls, we next varied them through the whole procedure on J_{H}4 (Figure S6). One control leaves no decoys, so the threshold falls back to Benjamini–Hochberg; it recalled 68% of planted lineage mutations, against 93% with two controls and 95% with three or four, with false-discovery proportions of 2.8–3.1% for the two- to four-control designs. All-null libraries yielded no calls with any number of controls (40 runs), and one control carrying recurrent artifacts changed false calls little, with or without the noisy-control rule. On Sμ, AID-null controls from a second experiment performed like the matched controls (66–68% versus 63% recall), and pooling all five lowered false calls from 2.2 to 0.8 per library.

Planted mutations lack the clonality and clustering of real SHM, so we also diluted real hypermutated reads into AID-null reads (Figure S7). On N114 V_{H}, mutation frequency was 0.87–0.97 of the expected value at 25–50% donor reads, and calls were made from 1–5% donor reads. On J_{H}4, in contrast, detection was all-or-nothing and depended on the donor: calls began at 2% donor reads for Wt3 and at 50% for Wt2, with no call below that.

Indels were validated in the same way, with ten planted insertions or deletions of 1–40 bp per library, supported by 1–20 reads, eight draws per control and error models fitted to the other controls. Among events supported by at least three reads, recall was 72% on J_{H}4 and 91% on N114 V_{H}, with 0.33 and zero false calls per library; events supported by one or two reads fall below the three-read requirement. Single-base homopolymer deletions in J_{H}4 were the least reliably recovered (19%), whereas recall was 100% for 2-bp insertions and 89% for deletions ≥10 bp (Figure S8).

We next simulated approximately 40 B-cell clones per J_{H}4 library, with clone sizes following a power-law distribution (Figure S9A). SHMtrace recalled 83% of single-read mutations versus 57% for Geneious, with FDP 0.037 versus 0.012 and 13.7 versus 4.0 false calls per library. In null libraries, false calls averaged 0.7 versus 4.3. When an unmutated clone contributed 60% of reads, read-weighted frequency was 6.2 versus a true 6.0 per 10^{3} bp, while the majority-rule clone-weighted measure recovered 94% of its corresponding true burden (14.6 versus 15.5; Figure S9B).

Because that dominant clone was unmutated, it could not trigger the ≥50% allele filter. When we repeated the simulation with a mutated dominant clone, nothing was lost at 40% abundance, but all mutations crossing the threshold at 60% or 80% were removed, and read-weighted and clone-weighted estimates fell by as much as 62% and 34%, respectively (STAR Methods).

At 500 reads per library, read-weighted mutation frequencies were within 2% of the simulated values (Figure S9C). Unique-variant density was less consistently recovered, because it counts each distinct substitution once: as depth increases, additional reads carry mutations already counted, enlarging the denominator without adding variants. Adding the aggregate estimate of uncalled single-read mutations restored 96–100% of the true density (Figures S9C and S9D). Comparisons of unique-variant density therefore require matched sequencing depth.

Finally, we asked whether the group tests hold their stated error rate. In 300 simulations per condition, with a between-animal coefficient of variation of 1, pooled-read tests returned p < 0.05 in 91% of 3-versus-3 and 94% of 5-versus-5 experiments without a true difference (Figure S9E), whereas negative-binomial rejection rates were 5.0% and 5.7%. With three animals per group, however, that test detected two-fold and four-fold changes in only 12% and 30% of simulations, illustrating the limited power at this sample size.
Matched controls set the background in real libraries

We next compared callers on real libraries with matched AID-null controls (Table S2; Figure 4). These included our J_{H}4 intron libraries from germinal-center B cells of three wild-type (Wt) and three *Aicda*^{−/−} mice, N114 hybridoma subclones transduced with AID or empty vector, and two loci in three assay contexts from an independent laboratory's public nanopore dataset: the Sμ switch region in LPS-activated B cells and in CH12 cells, and the AID off-target gene *Pim1*. Every caller analysed exactly the same reads (Table S3).

Across these assays, SHMtrace retained 1–4 calls in the three controls, compared with 5–20 for Geneious (Figures 4A–4E and 4G). As a result, geometric-mean unique-density separation, with zero-call controls assigned one-event values, reached 141-, 85-, 66- and 94-fold for J_{H}4, N114 V_{H}, primary-cell Sμ and CH12 Sμ, respectively, compared with 16–62-fold for Geneious and 2–40-fold for LoFreq configurations (Figure 4F). At 500 reads, J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} had reached 90% and 59% of the most each library yielded at any depth, without establishing saturation (Figures S10 and S11). Background mismatches were position-dependent, yet separable from the abundant clone-shared calls of Wt libraries (Figure S12).

Repertoire tools meet the same background from the other side. When the same N114 V_{H} reads were analyzed by IgBLAST[@ye2013] and SHazaM[@gupta2015], which count every mismatch to the germline (Figure S13), the AID libraries were only 2-fold above the empty-vector libraries with the IMGT germline, because the parental line differs from it (99.3% identity) and sequencing errors count as mutations. Using the parental V as germline raised this to 6-fold, and masking bases below Q20 to 32-fold, compared with 188-fold for SHMtrace.

Not every locus separated so clearly. At *Pim1*, mutation calls in AID-competent libraries remained close to the AID-null background: at 2,000 reads per library, SHMtrace yielded 1.8-fold separation, with four calls across the controls, compared with 1.6-fold and eleven control calls for Geneious. Increasing depth to all available reads (3,238–3,447 per library) did not clearly resolve the signal, with SHMtrace detecting 3–10 variants per AID-competent library and 0–3 per AID-null library, and Geneious 5–7 and 0–4, respectively (Table S1).

Two CH12 AID off-target loci, off-target 1 and off-target 2, then tested a genetic perturbation expected to reduce AID targeting[@seija2026]. Off-target 1 Wt libraries carried 69, 50, and 55 calls versus 0, 2, and 0 in *Aicda*^{−/−} controls, with densities of 3.07 versus 0.04 per 10^{5} bases (Welch p = 9.7 × 10^{−4} on log density). Off-target 2 counts were 42, 28, and 23 versus 2, 0, and 0, with densities of 1.68 versus 0.04 (p = 5.5 × 10^{−4}), and G:C substitutions accounted for 97% of calls at both loci. MLLT1/MLLT3 double knockout reduced counts to 2, 0, and 2 at off-target 1 (0.07 per 10^{5} bases) and 1, 0, and 0 at off-target 2 (0.02), with no detected difference from *Aicda*^{−/−} controls (p = 0.51 and 0.43). We report no fold here, because a zero-count convention would determine its magnitude.

These results depend on the error margin chosen from the controls. Without it, 5.4% of J_{H}4 and 9.6% of N114 V_{H} held-out control tests fell below p < 0.01; margins of five for the shared J_{H}4 window and ten for full-length J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} reduced these to 1.0%, 0.7% and 0.5%, respectively (Figure 4H). The margin calibrates the error model, whereas the separate decoy threshold estimates the false-discovery proportion.
SHMtrace-generated nanopore and Sanger profiles agree in matched mice

SHMtrace processed 182 Sanger chromatograms from the six nanopore-sequenced mice, retaining 134 clones after alignment and sequence-quality filtering for comparison across the shared 529-bp window (Figures 5 and S14). SHMtrace-derived mutation profiles distinguished Wt from *Aicda*^{−/−} mice on both platforms: Sanger showed 38-fold separation (p = 8.8 × 10^{−4}), and nanopore showed 141-fold separation when zero-call controls were assigned one event (p = 0.0027; Welch tests on log densities, n = 3 mice per group). Pooled substitution spectra were similar across the twelve substitution types (descriptive Pearson r = 0.92; slope = 0.97), as were positional profiles in 25-bp bins (r = 0.94). Among G:C mutations, 58% of Sanger and 54% of nanopore calls occurred at WRC/GYW hotspots, which accounted for 20% of eligible sites in the window. Among A:T mutations, 70% and 69%, respectively, occurred at WA/TW motifs, compared with 50% of eligible sites. No platform-by-substitution-type interaction was detected (p = 0.62), although this does not establish equivalence with three mice per group. Both densities count distinct variants but are not directly comparable: Sanger counts every Q≥20 change in 26–40 single clones, nanopore counts control-calibrated calls among 500 reads that resample expanded clones.
Sanger reanalysis recovers published comparisons and identifies discrepancies

We next re-analysed published Sanger data. A J_{H}4 study had compared four Wt and four *Maea*^{fl/fl}*Mb1*^{cre} mice with *Aicda*^{−/−} controls using SHMTool[@maccarthy2009,@barbulescu2024]. From its chromatograms, SHMtrace recovered a 4.6-fold frequency reduction, against 4.4-fold in the publication (one-tailed p = 2.3 × 10^{−4} and 0.0143; Figure S15). Spectra correlated at r = 0.99, and denominator-harmonized frequencies averaged 1.0-fold the published values. Shared trace assignments and identical mutated-clone pairs were retained as filed and flagged; the detailed discrepancies are in Table S4 and STAR Methods.

A second study from the same laboratory agreed on frequency but less closely on the knockout spectrum. Reanalysis of its 402 *Mkln1*-study chromatograms[@barbulescu2025] found an 8.0-fold frequency reduction versus the published 7.8-fold (p = 0.0038 and 0.014), and G:C transversions increased from 15% to 29%, against 16% to 27% in the published tables (p = 0.0078 and 0.0040). Spectrum correlations were r = 0.97 for Wt and 0.62 for knockout (Figure S16; Table S4).

Because both of those studies come from the laboratory that produced our libraries, we also re-analysed a Sanger study from an unrelated laboratory at a different locus. Thientosapol et al. hypermutated a SW_{HEL} V_{H}10 knock-in V region in germinal-centre B cells and deposited 1,795 sequences across five arms[@thientosapol2018] (Figure S17). From these records alone, SHMtrace counted 2,804 of the 2,809 mutations the study tabulates (r > 0.9999 across 60 spectrum cells), and mutations per sequence agreed to two decimal places in every arm. The four substitution classes the study tested moved as reported, and total mutation decreased in both analyses, although significance differed under the different tests used. Reassuringly, the *Msh2*^{−/−} arm, which SHMtrace was not told was a repair mutant, showed the expected collapse of A:T mutations. Because this study deposits sequences rather than chromatograms, it tests counting, spectra and group statistics but not trace reading.
Long reads retain whole-amplicon profiles and within-lineage linkage

Nanopore sequencing extended SHMtrace analysis of the J_{H}4 intron from the shared 529-bp Sanger window to a 1,141-bp interval spanning positions 90–1,230 (Figure 6A). Across this longer interval, Wt unique-variant density was 229-fold above controls. Approximately 69% of mutations occurred within the first 450 bp, with a seven-fold decline between the first and last 250 bp, consistent with the reported decline downstream of V(D)J[@lebecque1990]. Substitution spectra across the full interval closely matched those within the Sanger window (Pearson r = 0.989; Figure S18).

Wt mutations preferentially occurred at positions predicted to undergo SHM by the S5F model, which assigns mutability according to the surrounding five-base sequence. The targeting index, defined as mean predicted mutability at mutated positions divided by the mean across the analysis window, ranged from 1.22 to 1.36 (permutation p ≤ 0.015). Calls per position were also 4.1-fold higher in the highest-mutability quintile than in the lowest (Figure 6B). In contrast, *Aicda*^{−/−} mismatch positions showed no enrichment (index = 1.00; p = 0.50). Because S5F mutability is not used in the variant-calling test, this analysis provides a separate check that the detected mutations follow an SHM-associated targeting pattern.

Long reads also keep each molecule's junction, which groups reads into B-cell lineages (Figure 6C). In Wt2, one largely unmutated lineage accounted for 81% of junction-assigned reads, so the read-weighted frequency of 2.8 per 10^{3} bp rose to 16.3 when each lineage's majority-rule mutation profile was counted once. Wt3 and Wt4 changed less (22.5 to 24.9 and 4.9 to 5.3). The largest Wt3 lineage comprised 69 reads and four founder mutations, with five inferred sublineages extending to 17 mutations (Figure 6D). Without UMIs, however, PCR recombination and residual errors remain possible, so these are read-level reconstructions rather than proven cellular lineages.
Public datasets test transfer across platforms and experimental designs

To test transfer beyond nanopore, we analysed three public Illumina studies of different biological contexts (Figure 7). At J_{H}4 positions 53–122, Wt mice showed 56-fold greater mutation frequency than AID-null mice (log-rate Welch p = 0.005; n = 7 and 4), whereas *Ldha* deletion showed no detectable difference from Wt (Mann–Whitney p = 0.75), consistent with the original study[@sharma2023] (Figure 7A).

In *Aicda*^{−/−}*Ung*^{−/−}*Msh2*^{−/−} CH12F3 cells, ectopic AID increased frequency 40-fold over empty vector (p = 0.00781; n = 4 each), with one control call in 20,000 reads[@wang2023]. All AID calls were C→T/G→A, consistent with loss of uracil excision and mismatch repair; R50E yielded none (Figure 7B). R174E/R178E appeared more active but gave only 17% transitions, a 56% cluster within positions 164–172 and targeting index 0.73 versus 2.46 for AID. These features suggest a library-specific artifact absent from controls (Figure 7C). Establishing its source would require additional sequencing provenance or independent material.

HMCES-deficient Ramos clones[@wu2022] carried 3.8-fold more deletions and 2.5-fold more insertions than Wt clones (deletions, p = 1.0 × 10^{−4}; n = 6 per group; Figure 7D). Substitution calling in this deposit, however, depended strongly on one AID-null library, which a rule developed after inspecting this dataset excluded from threshold selection while retaining for model fitting (STAR Methods). Wt and HMCES-deficient clones then yielded 52–99 substitution calls each. That library's excess proved allelic rather than noise: every AID-null clone carries a second IGH allele near half its reads, which the 50% germline filter retains and phasing stripped from two clones but not the third. Masking such positions brings all twelve clones within 0.21–1.66 substitutions per 10^{3} bases, from a bimodal 0.4–0.8 and 3.8–8.2. The same rule also acted in the mOrange analysis.

A published mOrange reporter study compared active and catalytically inactive AID in cells carrying an empty vector, Ugi or UNG[@perezduran2012]. Using the inactive-AID libraries to calibrate calling, SHMtrace retained 115 substitutions, all at G:C and 75–100% at WRC/GYW hotspots (Figure 7E). Separation between active and inactive AID was 20-fold with empty vector, 1,002-fold with Ugi and 103-fold with UNG, with Ugi zeros assigned one event. Among retained substitutions, the transition share fell from 95% with Ugi to 4% with UNG, whereas uncorrected inactive-AID backgrounds contained 43–66% transitions. The paired mean difference was 92 percentage points (95% CI 74–110; paired t, p = 0.0021), although few calls per library limit precision.

Two engineered-diversification datasets extended the evaluation to mutations measured relative to experimental starting constructs (Figure S19). In a study using a common GFP substrate[@liu2018], no-editor libraries yielded at most one call in 20,000 reads. AID substitutions were more frequently located at WRC/GYW hotspots than APOBEC3A substitutions, both in Wt cells (56% versus 14%; p = 0.0040) and in UNG/MSH2-deficient cells (37% versus 20%; p = 9.0 × 10^{−4}). In the repair-deficient background, however, their transition shares were similar (78% versus 76%; p = 0.74), showing that transition enrichment alone could not distinguish the two enzymes.

The second engineered dataset, a CRISPR-X antibody-evolution study, diversified an antibody V_{H} and published the mutations it found in each selected cluster[@devilder2019]. Comparing the two lists position by position, SHMtrace recovered 150 of the 150 published mutations and called none the authors did not, across all 42 cluster entries (Figure S19B). Because the comparator is an independently curated list rather than another run of the same software, this is the sharpest available test of variant identity on this route.

Two further datasets tested transfer to another laboratory's switch-region libraries and to a fourth platform, and showed where a deposit limits what can be asked. Sμ libraries under PI3Kδ inhibition[@compagno2017] confound genotype with library layout: six of nine wild-type libraries are single-end whereas every *Aicda*^{−/−} library is paired, and the mates do not overlap, so only the twelve paired libraries reach the switch repeats where AID acts (Figure S20). Analysed over those repeats, the nine *Aicda*^{−/−} libraries returned one call between them against 81–172 per wild-type library (p = 0.0021), and the wild-type calls carried the AID signature: targeting index 1.52–1.67 and 31–35% C→T or G→A. The calibration therefore transfers to an independent laboratory, platform and perturbation. The drug comparison does not follow from this deposit, because only one wild-type replicate per treatment reaches the repeats.

Finally, PacBio Sμ–Sγ1 reads[@vincendeau2022] carry the donor, the join and the acceptor on one molecule, so we applied the junction module to a class-switch phenotype it was not tuned for (Figure S21). Mean microhomology was 1.01 nt in wild type and unchanged in *Shld1*^{−/−} (1.02 nt), but rose without XLF (1.69 nt) and in double mutants (1.59 nt), which also showed more ≥4-nt microhomology and fewer blunt junctions; *Shld1*^{−/−} junctions instead carried more insertions. This is the shift toward microhomology-mediated end joining expected when classical non-homologous end joining is impaired.

Measuring somatic hypermutation has long meant choosing between reading molecules accurately and reading enough of them. Our results suggest that this choice is no longer necessary, provided the background is measured rather than assumed. SHMtrace takes whatever a platform delivers, reads or chromatograms, and replaces the two assumptions that make low-frequency calling from single reads unreliable for SHM. First, rather than relying on quality scores alone, it estimates the background in the AID-null libraries that SHM studies already include, at the level of substitution type, strand and base quality, and checks that calibration by holding out each control in turn. Second, instead of treating reads as replicates, it tests independent biological samples. Both replacements held: 81% of planted J_{H}4 mutations and 90% on N114 V_{H} were recovered at false-discovery proportions near the default target, while a quality-based caller either missed most true mutations or, made permissive, called as much background as the uncorrected rule, and pooling reads produced false positives in more than 90% of simulated experiments without a true difference.

The gap this fills is specific, and it sits between two mature bodies of software. Repertoire toolkits identify and summarise mutations well: IgBLAST assigns germlines[@ye2013], Change-O and SHazaM quantify load[@gupta2015], SHMTool compares datasets[@maccarthy2009], and S5F models targeting[@yaari2013]. They begin, however, from mismatches already taken to be real, which is why counting every mismatch on the same N114 reads separated AID from empty-vector libraries by 2- to 32-fold, depending on germline and masking, where SHMtrace separated them by 188-fold. General-purpose variant callers do the opposite: they decide what is real, but from error models fitted to data of a different kind. LoFreq reads base qualities[@wilm2012], while ClairS and DeepSomatic were developed for tumour–normal sequencing, with different training data and calling assumptions[@zheng2026,@park2026]. As configured here, neither class measures what a particular SHM library does wrong. SHMtrace closes that circuit by making the AID-null control, where available, the source of the error model, and by carrying the measurement through to the animal-level comparison that the biology requires[@lazic2010]. Its distinctive contribution is therefore to connect control-informed mutation detection with interpretable profiles and comparisons across biological replicates in one reproducible workflow.

Seen this way, comparator performance is a matter of operating range rather than quality. LoFreq was designed for deep short-read data with calibrated qualities; its base-alignment correction suppressed nearly all nanopore calls here, and disabling it still limited recovery of low-support variants. That is not a defect on its intended data; rather, as configured here, it did not capture this assay's library-specific background as well as matched-control calibration did. The measurements suggest why. Above Q40, control error stopped decreasing and differed across the evaluated datasets (1–9 × 10^{−5}; Figure S3), so the quality score runs out of information exactly where SHM calling needs it. ClairS and DeepSomatic, similarly, recovered clean variants at higher allele fractions but few real SHM calls, and chemistry and model mismatches further qualify the external-data comparisons. Geneious, in turn, provided greater single-read recall on J_{H}4 and *Pim1* but more false calls on each amplicon. These are choices a study can make deliberately: sensitive mode raises the empirical target to 0.20 and recovers 72% of single-read mutations on J_{H}4 and 87% on N114 V_{H} at observed FDP 0.18 and 0.16, while events unresolved individually can still be estimated in aggregate.

Because the background is measured rather than modelled, one framework serves all four platforms, each through the analysis its data support. A Sanger clone is one molecule read once, so there is no read support to weigh against a background; the workflow therefore counts quality-filtered substitutions directly and reports the control-derived background beside them. Nanopore and Illumina libraries, by contrast, carry matched AID-null arms, so each candidate is tested against the errors those controls make. Nanopore spans the whole amplicon, which made the 3′ decline visible without tiling, identified clones from the V(D)J junction and ordered their mutations into trees; Illumina gives depth without that linkage. PacBio combines length with per-base accuracy, and reading the donor, the join and the acceptor on one molecule recovered a known end-joining phenotype from a deposit with no AID-null arm, using junction shape in place of calibrated calls. Figure S22 sets out what each measured. Agreement between platforms is itself evidence: nanopore and Sanger reads from the same six mice gave substitution spectra correlated at r = 0.92 and separated the genotypes in the same direction, supporting the use of cloning-free long reads to recover established SHM patterns while adding whole-amplicon linkage.

Applying the same engine to other laboratories' data turned out to be a harder test than any internal benchmark. Published sequence collections support reproducible reanalysis when clones are linked to animals and genotypes: SHMtrace recovered the principal J_{H}4 frequency and G:C comparisons, matched SW_{HEL} counts across five arms and twelve substitution types (2,804 of 2,809 tabulated mutations; r > 0.9999), and recovered 150 of 150 mutations an antibody-evolution study curated by hand, calling none its authors did not. Agreement was not complete, and the exceptions are as informative: Wt frequencies differed after denominator harmonisation, the published *Mkln1* A:T decrease was not significant in the reanalysis, and the SW_{HEL} total-mutation inference differed under a different test (Tables S4 and S5; Figures S15–S17). The Sanger re-analysis also surfaced bookkeeping problems, which SHMtrace now checks and reports rather than silently resolving.

What this enables in practice is a short experiment-to-answer path that keeps its own evidence: read accounting, fixed-seed sampling and one engine behind the desktop and command-line interfaces, with every exclusion, threshold and flagged site written out for inspection. The power analysis sets the honest expectation. How many animals a study needs depends on the difference it seeks: under variation estimated from three Wt J_{H}4 mice, the AID-competent against AID-null contrasts made here separate at three animals per group, whereas a two-fold difference between two AID-proficient groups would require about 24, and more if three mice underestimate the variation (Figure S9F). Sequencing depth cannot substitute for independent biological samples, and no analysis can recover a comparison the design did not support. Within that boundary, however, the framework extends readily. It needs only a target, matched AID-null libraries and a sample sheet, which is why it could be applied to off-target loci, switch regions, engineered diversification and base-editor substrates across twelve loci from eleven laboratories. Further validation on independently prepared runs and UMI-tagged SHM libraries will establish how far it extends. More broadly, SHMtrace offers a practical foundation for studying how AID targeting and DNA repair shape antibody diversification.

SHMtrace relies on representative AID-null controls prepared and sequenced alongside the samples. Error profiles can vary between runs and basecalling configurations, and calibration using controls from a different run was not evaluated. With one nanopore run per assay, the present results do not establish performance across independent runs.

The reported variants remain subject to technical uncertainty. Without UMIs, early PCR errors, recombination and repeated sequencing of PCR-derived molecules cannot be reliably distinguished from genuine mutations or expanded biological lineages. Mutation trees therefore describe relationships among reads rather than independently established cellular lineages. The default ≥50% allele-frequency filter can also remove genuine mutations shared by a dominant lineage. Excluded sites are reported for review, and experiments with a known starting sequence can use an optional reference policy that retains high-frequency differences. Single-read mutations that cannot be called individually are estimated only in aggregate, and unique-variant densities require comparison at matched sequencing depth.

The empirical false-discovery estimate depends on the available controls and can exceed its nominal target when background differs between libraries. Noisy-control exclusion requires at least three controls, and its effect should be reviewed. Sample-specific artifacts absent from the controls may still pass the test; spectrum and clustering flags can identify unusual patterns but require interpretation. At weakly mutated targets such as Pim1, signal remained close to background.

The core validation used three animals per group for J_{H}4 and one locus per cell system. Settings were developed using these libraries and applied to public datasets without dataset-specific retuning, although the noisy-control exclusion rule was introduced after inspection of the Ramos results. Evaluation on an independent sequencing run with new biological samples would provide a stronger test of generalizability. Indel validation comprised nanopore spike-ins and one Illumina biological phenotype, while UMI validation used rRNA rather than SHM data. These experiments do not establish performance on biological nanopore indels or UMI-tagged SHM libraries; molecule-level consensus remains preferable when available. Two Sanger studies originated from the authors’ laboratory, while the independent Sanger study provided sequences without chromatograms or AID-null controls. Together, these datasets evaluate distinct parts of the workflow, with different limits on the conclusions each can support.

The N114 line carries a fixed, rearranged heavy-chain V region of the J558/IGHV1 family: IgBLAST assigns it to IGHV1-47-36 with IGHD1-1 and IGHJ3, and germline sequence of that V gene matches it over the whole V segment, so the assignment does not rest on this analysis. Relative to that germline the line carries two changes in CDR2, in frame and confirmed by the reads: the first replaces the germline glycine with an opal stop (TGA) and the second changes the following glycine to valine, giving W-I-Y-P-stop-N-V-N-T-K in place of W-I-Y-P-G-N-G-N-T-K. The stop is the point of the line: it prevents antibody production, and the original study scored its reversion as hypermutation[@martin2002]. Sequencing supersedes that readout: the analysis here measures mutation across the whole V region rather than reversion at one codon, and is made against the line's own reference throughout, which carries the stop; the V region is called N114 V_{H} rather than by an allele. The 1,230-bp J_{H}4 intron amplicon[@jolly1997,@barbulescu2024] and the 655-bp N114 V-region amplicon[@martin2002] were amplified with Platinum SuperFi II high-fidelity DNA polymerase. SHMtrace reads FASTQ files, which may be gzipped or, for Illumina data, paired files that are merged on their overlap. Reads are then processed in the following order. First, reads longer than a locus-specific limit (2,000 bp for J_{H}4 and 900 bp for N114 V_{H}) are removed, as are reads with a mean expected error above 0.01 per base, calculated from Phred qualities[@edgar2015]. Second, reads are aligned with minimap2 (map-ont preset, or sr for Illumina) against an index containing the target and any competing references, and each read is assigned to the sequence it aligns to best. Unmapped reads, reads assigned to a competing reference, reads with a supplementary alignment (chimeras), and reads aligned over less than a minimum length (800 bp for J_{H}4 and 400 bp for N114 V_{H}) are removed. For J_{H}4, the competing references were a J_{H}4-like paralog (the consensus of Agouti-type clones, approximately 12% divergent) and a recurrent contaminant haplotype. Because a full-length paralog read can align better to the longer target, reads carrying 10 or more bases specific to a competing reference, at sites where fewer than 20% of the sample's reads carry them, are also removed. Genuine J_{H}4 reads carry 0–7 such bases, whereas paralog reads and chimeras carry 11–62. The fate of every read is recorded. Usable reads were then downsampled at random with a fixed seed (Python random, seed 0) to the analysis depth: 500 reads for J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} and 2,000 reads for the IRCM loci. The analysis windows were positions 101–629 (529 bp, the window shared with Sanger) or 90–1,230 (full length) of the J_{H}4 reference and positions 21–635 of the N114 V_{H} reference. For loci whose window is not set by a preset, it runs from position 21 to 20 bases before the reference's end: Sμ 21–631 (611 bp), *Pim1* 21–882 (862 bp), off-target 1 21–988 (968 bp) and off-target 2 21–962 (942 bp). Reads that align better to a paralog, are chimeric or carry paralog-specific bases are removed, and the same number of usable reads is then drawn from every library. Read preparation removed 67% of delivered J_{H}4 reads overall (Figure S2A), and competitive alignment alone was not enough: without an additional paralog-base filter, simulated paralog reads produced 35–54 false variants per library.

Each observed single-nucleotide difference within the window is a candidate, including substitutions supported by one read. Control error rates are estimated by substitution type, strand and quality threshold, combining a pooled rate with position-specific counts. For a candidate with k supporting reads ranked q_{1} ≥ q_{2} ≥ …, the test evaluates, for each j ≤ k, the probability of at least j errors with quality ≥qj, using strand-specific depth and control rates multiplied by margin c. The reported p value is the smallest tail probability multiplied by k.

The margin c is chosen by leaving one control out at a time. It is an empirical calibration factor: it does not imply that sequencing errors are five or ten times the fitted rate, and it does not by itself set the false-discovery level, which the decoy threshold addresses separately. Because the same few controls choose the margin and supply the decoys, the false-discovery estimate is conditional on how well they represent the samples' background; it is not a guarantee. Each control is tested against an error model built from the other controls, and c is the smallest value in the grid 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50 at which no more than 1% of candidate tests pooled across held-out controls reach p < 0.01. In the analyses reported here, c was 5× on J_{H}4, 10× on the full length, and 10× on N114 V_{H}. The same held-out tests, made at the samples' analysis depth, are then used to set the significance threshold. Each held-out control is kept as a decoy, defined by its sorted p values and the number of bases it tested. For a sample and a candidate threshold t, the expected number of false calls is the mean, across decoys, of the number of decoy p values ≤ t, scaled by the ratio of the sample's tested bases to the decoy's when that ratio exceeds 1. Decoys are never scaled down to a shallower library, whose coarser p values they would otherwise underestimate. SHMtrace keeps the largest t at which the expected number of false calls is at most 0.05 times the number of sample p values ≤ t, an empirical false-discovery estimate inspired by target–decoy analysis[@elias2007]. A control is never used as its own decoy: when a control is tested, only the other controls serve as decoys. Each sample is judged against the controls of its own sequencing run when that run has at least two (one, for a control), and against all controls otherwise, with the report naming any sample whose run has no control; every J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} sample shared its controls' run, while the public deposits do not record runs, so their samples were judged against all of their study's controls. A control whose held-out candidates at p ≤ 0.01 per base exceed five times the median of the other controls, and number at least five, is left out of the decoys (unless no decoy would remain) and named in the report; it still contributes to the error model, and is never removed from the analysis. The comparison needs a majority to judge against, so it is made only when at least two other controls remain, that is with three or more controls; with exactly two, the more variable library is named in the report but not left out, because which of the two is unusual cannot be established. The rule was written for one public dataset, the Ramos clones of Figure 7D, in which a single *Aicda*^{−/−} clone suppressed every call — a clone whose excess was later traced to a second IGH allele the phasing step removed from its two peers and retained in it, rather than to a difference in sequencing noise; it was then applied to the other datasets and was already fixed when the off-target libraries were analyzed, where it excluded no control; it excluded one in the mOrange analysis. It is therefore a rule derived from data rather than a pre-registered one, and it is reported here so that its effect can be judged. With fewer than two controls, or for indels, the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure[@benjamini1995] across positions and alternative alleles is used instead. The number of controls therefore selects between four modes, and the output records which was used in its `multiple_testing` field, so a reader never has to infer it. With **no control** the background is not measured at all: every candidate is judged from base qualities, the correction is Benjamini–Hochberg, indels are not called, and the run carries a note saying so. With **one control** that library supplies the error model, but the margin cannot be fitted by leaving a control out and the default of 10, measured on J_{H}4, is used; a control cannot be its own decoy, so there is no decoy set and the correction is again Benjamini–Hochberg; the noisy-control rule cannot act, since it needs two others to compare against. With **two** each is the other's decoy, the margin is fitted but can reach the top of its grid, and a disagreement between the pair is reported without acting on it, because with two there is no majority to say which is wrong. With **three or more** the margin is fitted by leave-one-out, the decoys are the peers, and a far noisier control is set aside automatically. A single control is enough to run but not to calibrate: the model fitted to that one library can absorb the signal, so results from it should be reported as mismatch rates without an FDR claim. Benjamini–Hochberg is not avoided because the p values are discrete: it controls the false-discovery rate for valid discrete p values, conservatively. It is avoided because of how candidates arise. A position enters the test only when at least one read already differs from the reference there, so the tested set is chosen by the same data that supply the evidence, and the null distribution of a candidate's p value is conditioned on that selection rather than superuniform on (0, 1]. The control-based threshold applies the same candidate-selection rule to samples and held-out controls, so it measures the corresponding background empirically. This does not establish formal FDR control: the decoys are few, their fitted nulls differ from the sample null, and their exchangeability with samples is an assumption. Figure S23 tests selected consequences of these limitations, and Figure S5 compares the target with the realised proportion on planted truth: the default was met when pooled, and targets below it were not; Figure S6 varies the number and source of the controls. Because the threshold targets a proportion, a library with many true mutations admits more false calls in absolute terms: in simulated polyclonal lineages, 13.7 per library, in exchange for recalling 83% of single-read mutations. Table S7 compares the default with a target of 0.01 and with the noisiest control's decoy count in place of the mean. At 0.01, false calls in those lineages fell to 3.0 per library but single-read recall fell to 38%; on the planted J_{H}4 controls, recall fell from 81% to 17% without a lower false-discovery proportion (0.061), whereas N114 V_{H} kept 76% recall at 0.005. With three controls, the decoy counts are too coarse to resolve a 1% target reliably. In the J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} projects, both stricter settings removed calls only from mutation-bearing libraries; the group differences remained 71–138-fold (p ≤ 0.0078). The default was kept. Alternative alleles carried by at least 50% of covering reads are removed as germline or parental differences; other alleles at the same position remain eligible. Without controls, recommended mode uses a Poisson approximation to read-quality error probabilities; the separate pbinom mode implements the exact Poisson-binomial calculation.

Repair interpretations in *Ung*^{−/−}*Msh2*^{−/−} cells and Ugi/UNG fibroblasts are therefore grounded in the experimental perturbations rather than inferred from spectra alone.
