Testing the calling procedure as a whole

End-to-end assessment used partitions and planted mutations from three existing *Aicda*^{−/−} J_{H}4 libraries (`crm/fdr_validation.py`). Cases used KO1 reads. Two-control analyses used one partition each from KO2/KO3; three-control analyses used two KO2 partitions and one KO3 partition. Case/control sets shared no read records, but without UMIs this does not establish original-molecule independence. Partitions are technical resamples rather than independent biological controls. Each `run_project` analysis reselected its margin, threshold and exclusions. Conditions were unmodified background, one noisy control, case-only artifact and shared case/control artifact. Artifacts occupied six positions at nominal 6% support; shared artifacts used identical alternate alleles, and case artifacts avoided planted biological sites. Control number (two/three), depth (250/500/1,000) and mutation burden (none/approximately 400 true recovered calls) were varied. Exclusion-on/off analyses used identical inputs (Figure S23). These stress tests assess behavior conditional on existing libraries, not transfer to a new run.

Under unmodified all-null background, discoveries occurred in 1/25 exclusion-on and 0/25 exclusion-off resamples; with one noisy control, both were 0/25. Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bounds of 20% and 14% for the unmodified condition do not establish a 5% bound. Shared-artifact resamples yielded 0/5 discoveries in both settings, each with a 52% upper bound. Case-only artifacts yielded discoveries in 5/5 under both settings, averaging 6.0 false calls. With biological mutations and exclusion enabled, mean per-library FDP was 3.8%, 3.0%, 3.7% and 5.1% for unmodified, noisy-control, shared-artifact and case-only conditions, respectively (five resamples each). Per-library FDP, pooled false/(true+false), and the all-null probability of any discovery are reported separately. These small conditional experiments do not establish general error control.

The noisy control was excluded in 25/25 all-null rule-on resamples. With biological mutations, exclusion-on/off analyses averaged 396.0/394.2 true calls and 12.2/11.2 false calls across five paired resamples. At least three controls are required to assess an outlier against peers. When the peer median is zero, ≥5 held-out candidates at p≤0.01 trigger exclusion; an unmodified control was consequently excluded in 3/25 all-null resamples. Every exclusion is recorded and warrants review, including sensitivity to retaining that control.

The default mean-decoy estimator was compared with `control_decoy_estimate="max"`, which requires the threshold to satisfy the noisiest retained decoy (`crm/fdr_estimator.py`). On unmodified mutation-bearing inputs, mean FDP was 3.8% versus 2.5%, with 403.0 versus 389.0 true calls. For case-only artifacts, FDP was 5.1% versus 4.1%. Five paired resamples per condition used identical inputs. This compares implemented estimators; it is neither independent validation nor proof that the maximum guarantees FDR control.

Reported runtimes are wall-clock seconds for one `run_project` call on an Apple M2 Pro (12 cores, 32 GB; macOS), from prepared input to written results. They include file reading, mappy alignment, calling and sample summaries, but exclude reference construction and external benchmark containers. Sanger projects contain a few hundred chromatograms; nanopore projects contain six libraries analyzed at 500–2,000 reads. Input recovery and curation, including reconstruction of clone assignments from historical projects, took substantially longer and are excluded from compute times.
The Geneious rule was reproduced as an uncorrected approximate p ≤ 0.05 per candidate, which matched Geneious exports site by site (Jaccard index 0.97–0.98 on Wt J_{H}4).

Three measures are reported per library, and they answer different questions; group tests then use one value per animal. A unique variant is a position and substituted base counted once per library, however many reads carry it; unique means distinct within that library and does not imply an independent mutational origin, since one lineage's trunk mutation is one unique variant. **Unique-variant density** is D / B × 10^{5}, where D is the number of unique variants and B the base observations at callable positions (inside the analysis window and the end trims), counted exactly as the read depth summed over those positions, not the number of reference positions. Because B grows with depth while D saturates, this density falls as depth rises even at a constant mutation rate, so it is compared only between libraries analyzed at the same depth (Figure S11). **Read-weighted mutation frequency** is Σ m_{i} / (N × L) × 10^{3}, where m_{i} is the number of called sites read i carries at or above the configured minimum base quality (0 for these read-library analyses), N the reads analyzed and L the window length; a mutation shared by many reads is counted once in each of them, so an expanded clone raises it. This fixed-window frequency credits every read with the whole window; an observed-base frequency, which counts only the bases each read covers, is reported beside it and agrees when reads span the window, as they did in the J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} projects to within 2.4%. **Clone-weighted frequency** groups reads by their V(D)J junction, keeps a mutation when at least half the reads of its clone carry it (any read of a single-read clone), and is Σ c_{k} / (K × L) × 10^{3} over the K clones, so each clone counts once whatever its size. For wild-type J_{H}4 library Wt2 at 500 reads over the 529-bp window these give 221 unique variants over 263,886 base observations (83.8 × 10^{−5}), 747 read-level mutations over 264,500 bases (2.82 × 10^{−3}), and 207 clonal mutations over 24 clones (16.3 × 10^{−3}); the clone-weighted value is the largest because one clone holds 81% of the reads. For Sanger clones, where each clone is one molecule read once, the frequency denominator is the clones analyzed times L, with L the 529-bp window; the published studies used their own full consensus length and counted every filed clone, which is the convention Table S4 reports separately.

Two implementation details of the error model. The rate used at a site is the pooled rate for that substitution, strand and quality over all window positions, used as a floor, with that position's own control count shrunk toward it by m = 500 pseudo-observations, so a position the controls show erring often keeps its high rate while a position that happened to show none does not look error-free. A substitution class the controls never showed is given half a pseudo-count over the control bases observed, which keeps the quality tail above zero rather than allowing a p value of exactly zero. Indels are called separately, because nanopore indel errors are systematic rather than quality-driven: each exact indel is tested against the rate of its class (insertion or deletion, length up to 4, homopolymer run up to 5), counted per read spanning each position of the analysis window and used as a floor, with that site's own control rate shrunk toward it and inflated by a margin fitted as the substitution margin is; candidates are corrected by Benjamini–Hochberg; indels are counted only at quality ≥ 30 at the inserted bases or the bases flanking a deletion, and those carried by fewer than three reads are not called. UMI consensus groups reads by their tags, allowing up to 3 edits per tag end, greedily from the most abundant tag and merging a neighbor only when it is at most half as abundant; groups of fewer than 3 reads are dropped, and each remaining group becomes one quality-weighted consensus read. The single-read estimate divides the excess of single-read substitutions at quality ≥ 35 over the controls' rate by the share of that sample's correctly read bases reaching that quality, so that the estimate does not depend on the cutoff; that it does not between Q30 and Q40 is the check reported for J_{H}4.
Single-read estimate, clones, mutation trees, and quality checks

Single-read mutations not called individually are estimated in aggregate. SHMtrace counts Q≥35 single-read substitutions outside the accepted call set, subtracts the control expectation scaled to sample bases, and divides by the fraction of correctly read bases reaching that quality. Control events are counted only at positions and alleles where the sample could show a single-read event, so neither its per-site calls nor alleles it carries in two or more reads add to the background. The 95% interval inverts a profile likelihood in which the sample count is Poisson in signal plus background and the control count Poisson in background, scaled by the between-control overdispersion; it stays nonzero when neither sample nor controls show an event. In simulation it covered the true count in 92.5–98.8% of experiments with Poisson background, and in 87–90% when three heterogeneous controls carried several background events, because three controls estimate the overdispersion imprecisely. The combined density's interval holds the per-site calls fixed.

Two different things are called a clone in this field, and this paper keeps them apart. A *Sanger clone* is one bacterial colony, that is one PCR product carried by one transformant and sequenced once: a unit of sequencing, which says nothing about which B cell the molecule came from, and two Sanger clones of one animal may well come from the same B cell lineage. A *B cell clone* is a lineage, defined here by a shared V(D)J junction, which is what the clone-weighted frequency and the mutation trees use. The two coincide only by accident. Where the text says a measure counts each clone once, it means the B cell clone; the Sanger denominator is clones analyzed × 529 bp, where those clones are the sequencing units. Sanger amplicons of the J_{H}4 intron do not span the junction, so B cell clones cannot be identified in them, and clone-weighted frequencies are reported only for the nanopore libraries.

Junction grouping uses the twenty bases immediately upstream of alignment starts occurring within 18 bp of J_{H}4. Sequences are clustered greedily around abundance-ranked centroids with edit distance ≤3 and a free 5′ end. Each lineage's majority profile retains calls supported by at least half its reads. Tree nodes merge mutations supported by ≥2 lineage reads with Jaccard overlap ≥0.9; each node's parent is the smallest node containing ≥90% of its supporting reads. A read fits when its nodes occupy one ancestral path. The four-gamete test requires each of the four presence/absence combinations for a mutation pair in at least two reads. Overall, 70% of mutated reads fitted one tree, and 7/1,128 mutation pairs failed the four-gamete test.

The targeting index is mean S5F mutability[@yaari2013] at mutated positions divided by the window mean. A one-sided permutation test uses 2,000 random position sets; the model was exported from SHazaM 1.2.0. Positional-clustering flags identify 10-base windows with more calls than expected under a Poisson distribution, with Bonferroni correction across windows (p < 10^{−3}). Figure S24 summarizes the workflow; Figure S25 illustrates the analytical rules using J_{H}4 libraries. Sanger traces are assigned through a sample sheet and trimmed to their longest reliably aligned Q≥20 segment. All Q≥20 substitutions are counted after germline filtering. Quality-control flags identify copied files, unexpectedly shared clones between animals (Poisson test weighted by mutation frequency across animals), excess mutations in controls, label mismatches and mutation-load outliers. Flags are reported for review without automatic exclusion. These flags were tested on forty simulated projects, each carrying one instance of every bookkeeping error: a changed label was detectable only where the affected clones shared mutations with another animal's clones, because a label alone leaves no trace in the sequence, and no correctly assigned clone was flagged in error among the 6,018 tested (`crm/sanger_validation_summary.json`).

The Sanger route counts Q≥20 substitutions without per-call significance testing. AID-null clones provide the observed Q≥20 mismatch rate after their own germline differences are excluded, stratified by quality and position. Applying these rates to each sample's bases gives the expected background count, reported beside observations without subtraction. Sites mismatched in more than one control clone are annotated on corresponding sample calls. This background estimate contextualizes Sanger counts but does not determine acceptance of individual substitutions.

For the Maea Sanger study[@barbulescu2024], chromatograms from four 96-well plates and the pilot plate of cohort two were downloaded from the sequencing facility portal. Mouse assignments were reconstructed from the original project folders using screen recordings. Four traces filed under two mice were retained under both assignments. Published per-mouse values came from Source Data: Figure 2h for mutation frequencies, including *Aicda*^{−/−} mice; Figure 2i for G:C transitions and transversions; and Figure 2g for clone distributions. Twelve-type counts were transcribed from Supplementary Figure 9b, using printed cell values where they conflicted with printed totals. Wt and *Maea*-deficient groups were compared using the original one-tailed unpaired t test; comparisons with *Aicda*^{−/−} used Welch tests on log frequencies. Data S1 contains the sample sheet and transcribed tables.

For the *Mkln1* study[@barbulescu2025], mouse assignments were reconstructed from original project folders using a screen recording. A separate folder contained 58 later-run *Mkln1*^{−/−} traces named for the same three mice. These were included under their named mice because the published substitution counts exceed the earlier preprint by eight mutations, matching the number and types of SHMtrace calls in this batch. The files do not establish which later clones entered the published tables or how the three knockout folders map to published mice #1–#3; comparisons therefore use groups rather than matched mice. Each later clone carries at most two mutations and cannot be placed using the matched nanopore libraries, because assignment requires a read carrying at least three of its mutations.

A sensitivity analysis used an evidence-based *Mkln1* clone set with rules fixed before analysis and independent of published values. Paralog amplicons and trace copies were set aside as in the primary analysis. Lineages filed under two mice, identified by duplicate-clone and shared-mutation checks, were sought in matched J_{H}4 nanopore libraries after excluding positions mismatched in >0.5% of *Aicda*^{−/−} reads. A read supported a lineage when it carried more than half its shared mutations and at least three. Lineages supported by at least three reads in exactly one mouse library were reassigned to that mouse; other multiply filed lineages were set aside. AID-null clones flagged for more mutations than predicted by their base qualities would also have been excluded; none met this criterion. Clones without an original mouse assignment remained excluded, as in the primary analysis.

For the SW_{HEL} study[@thientosapol2018], all 1,795 GenBank clones (MH198782–MH200576) were downloaded and treated as Sanger sequences; the sample sheet records each accession, host and well. GenBank provides no base qualities, so Q30 was assigned as a processing convention rather than measured quality. The majority-consensus reference converged in two iterations. The analysis window covered the interval represented in ≥99% of clones (558 bp of the 576-bp consensus). Host and genotype assignments followed deposited records, with the UGI group kept separate. No *Aicda*^{−/−} group was available for background estimation. Published per-group counts were transcribed from the source study's Table 1, which counts each sequence independently. SHMtrace totals were compared using this convention; unique-mutation counts are lower, as expected. The publication lists 1,796 sequences versus 1,795 deposited, owing to one fewer *Msh2*^{−/−} record (445 versus 446); no deposited record was excluded. The Wt deposit names twelve hosts versus thirteen reported, and AT40 contains 88 clones, approximately twice the other collections, suggesting that two animals may share this label. Pooled counts are unaffected. Animal-level tests use deposited host names and were repeated without AT40; clones were not arbitrarily split between inferred animals. Excluding AT40 gave p = 1.6 × 10^{−10}, 8.5 × 10^{−6}, 5.0 × 10^{−10}, and 0.18 for the four substitution classes and 2.6 × 10^{−4} for total mutation, versus 9.7 × 10^{−11}, 7.7 × 10^{−6}, 1.2 × 10^{−10}, 0.14 and 3.8 × 10^{−4} with all hosts.

The high-allele-fraction rule removes any change carried by at least 50% of the reads covering it, as a germline or parental difference. Because a mutation shared by a dominant lineage reaches the same frequency, we measured what the rule costs by simulating lineages whose dominant clone is itself mutated. Libraries were built on the J_{H}4 AID-null reads as for Figure S9A, with the dominant clone holding 40%, 60% or 80% of the reads and carrying its own trunk mutations (mean 6, as the other clones), 3 libraries per abundance, each planted library called with the other two controls as its null. A planted mutation was counted as exposed to the rule when the reads carrying it reached the threshold at its position. At 40% none did. At 60% and 80%, 0–4 and 0–4 per library did, and none of them was called: a mutation at or above the threshold is removed before any test. Across libraries the read-weighted frequency fell to as much as 40% and 62% below the truth and the clone-weighted frequency to 26% and 34%, while libraries in which nothing crossed the threshold were unaffected. Each sample's report now lists every site the rule removed with its read count, depth and frequency, so a library with a large mutated clone can be recognized and its sites inspected. The rule has the opposite failure as well: a difference carried by one of two alleles sits near half the reads and can fall either side of the threshold, so a clonal line heterozygous across the sequenced region can have that second allele tested as if it were somatic. `mask_control_het` addresses this from the controls. A position and alternative allele that any control library reads in at least `control_het_min_frequency` (0.25) of its reads, up to the 50% rule, over at least `control_het_min_depth` (20) reads, is treated as a second allele there and is left out of the samples' candidates and of the controls' decoys alike, so both sides lose the same sites; the count is reported as `control_het_removed`. One control is enough to establish a site, so a variant private to one library is caught, and sequencing error does not reach a quarter of the reads at a covered position; what the rule can lose is a real mutation that a control also carries at that level. It is off by default, so no result reported here uses it, and it is off under `ancestral_reference`, where a change driven high is the experiment's subject. Run over the controls of the ten sets that have three or more mutation-free controls, it sets aside sites in two, the Illumina Ramos VDJ (29 sites) and the public nanopore Sμ CH12 libraries (2), and none in the other eight, this study's own J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} among them. On the Ramos deposit it removes 55 calls from seven of the twelve Wt and HMCES-deficient clones, 42 of them carried by 43–49% of reads at nine positions.

For the matched-platform comparison, 184 traces were assigned to the six mice, 2 excluded in the sample sheet and 182 processed; 48 failed analysis and 134 were retained (Figure S14). This distinguishes the complete 447-trace archive from the matched comparison.

In matched mice, G:C hotspot shares were 58% for Sanger and 54% for nanopore versus 20% of eligible positions; A:T shares were 70% and 69% versus 50%. No equivalence conclusion follows from the non-significant interaction at n=3. In the independent SW_{HEL} comparison, the analysis window was 558 bp; per-class p-values were 9.7 × 10^{−11}, 7.7 × 10^{−6}, 1.2 × 10^{−10} and 0.14. The published total-mutation p=0.07 used one-way ANOVA; the reanalysis p=3.8 × 10^{−4} used per-animal log-rate Welch. The deposit's 12 hosts differ from the reported 13; the potentially pooled host was retained and excluded in sensitivity analysis. A:T mutation shares fell from 56% in Wt to 5% in *Msh2* mutants.

SHMtrace processed 293 chromatograms in 16 s after manual assignment curation. G:C transitions fell from 19% to 11% (same published shares; p=2.9 × 10^{−4} versus 0.0028 published), while transversions rose from 15% to 21% versus 14% to 20% published (p=0.025 versus 0.0285). Mouse rankings correlated at ρ=0.95. Controls had two mutations in 19 clones (p=3.0 × 10^{−4} versus Wt and 0.0039 versus knockout). Shared trace assignments and 134 identical mutated-clone pairs remained as filed and were flagged.

Figure 4 and Table S1 are built by `crm/benchmark_real.py`, which drives the calling stage directly so that every caller sees exactly the same reads; the product itself runs `run_project`. Because those are two code paths, they were compared library by library (`crm/route_check.py`). On the J_{H}4 and N114 V_{H} libraries of this study the two agree exactly, all twelve giving identical calls. On the four public nanopore datasets they do not, because the leave-one-control-out margin is fitted over a different set: the benchmark route fits it from the two peers of each held-out control, `run_project` across all three together, so the thresholds differ. Counts then move in both directions, for instance 88 against 101 calls in one Sμ wild-type library and 6 against 1 in one *Pim1* wild type. The separations are unchanged in direction and in order of magnitude under either route (J_{H}4 141 against 141, N114 V_{H} 85 against 84, Sμ LPS 66 against 84, Sμ CH12 94 against 171, off-target 1 53 against 46, off-target 2 28 against 24), and *Pim1* stays below separation either way, at 1.8 against 0.8. Figure 4 therefore reports the benchmark route throughout, for comparability between callers, and Table S3 reports `run_project`, where the two coincide.

For each library, the reads analyzed by SHMtrace were written out, aligned with minimap2 using the same preset with secondary alignments turned off, and sorted and indexed with SAMtools. They were then called with LoFreq 2.1.5 `call`, restricted to the analysis window, at three settings: default settings (base-alignment quality on, Bonferroni correction, default filters); `-B` (base-alignment quality off); and `-B -a 0.05 -b 1 --no-default-filter` (uncorrected p ≤ 0.05, filters off). Substitutions at an allele frequency below 0.5 were kept, matching SHMtrace's germline filter, and all callers used the same density denominator for each library. In the spike-in tests, 60 sites per replicate were chosen with WRC/GYW motifs weighted 4-fold and WA/TW motifs 2-fold, and each substitution was written into 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, or 20 reads covering that site while keeping each read's own base quality. Three replicates were performed for each held-out control. Two ablations used the same planted libraries (`crm/spikein.py --profiles ctlnull_bh,qualonly_pbinom --tag _ablation`; Table S1): ctlnull_bh tests each site against its per-position error rate in the other controls with Benjamini–Hochberg correction, without quality calibration or the decoy threshold, and qualonly_pbinom applies the exact Poisson-binomial test to read qualities with no control null. In these runs the recommended mode reproduced the original spike-in results exactly. For Figure S5 the same libraries were called at target false-discovery rates of 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.30 (`fdr_alpha`), every other setting at its default; the realised proportion is false calls over all calls, pooled over a locus's libraries. For Figure S6 (`crm/controls_design.py`), the validation libraries of Figure S23 (KO1 carrying planted polyclonal lineages, or none, against halves of KO2 and KO3) were run through `run_project` with one to four controls, and with one control carrying recurrent artifacts, 10 repeats per setting; the third and fourth controls are halves of the same two animals. Each Sμ LPS AID-null library, with 60 planted substitutions and three draws, was called against its experiment's other two controls, two or three CH12 AID-null controls, or all five. The SRA reads carry no run identifiers, so this compares experiments, not verified sequencing runs. For the dilution series (`crm/titration.py`), 500 usable reads were drawn with a fraction f from an AID-active library and the rest from one AID-null library (J_{H}4 KO1; N114 D1), 3 draws per fraction, and called by `run_project` against the other two AID-null libraries; expected mutation frequency is f times the donor at f = 1 plus (1 − f) times the diluent. N114 V_{H} used `ancestral_reference`, because its reference is the parental construct: with the default 50% rule, mutations fixed within a subclone are removed at f = 1 but counted once diluted, and D3 then read 1.84 per 10^{3} bp at f = 0.5 and 0.63 at f = 1. For Figure S13 (`crm/immcantation_compare.py`), the 500 reads SHMtrace analyzed from each N114 V_{H} library were passed to IgBLAST 1.22.0 (AIRR output) against the IMGT mouse IGH germlines, or with the parental V segment (294 bp) as the only V germline, with and without bases below Q20 replaced by N first (the rule of pRESTO's quality masking). SHazaM `observedMutations` counted substitutions between `v_sequence_alignment` and `v_germline_alignment`; a library's value is the mean over reads. SHMtrace's value is the supporting reads of its calls in the same segment over analyzed reads times its length. MiXCR was not run. The IRCM runs (PRJNA1481264) were downloaded with the SRA Toolkit, validated with vdb-validate, and subsampled to 6,000 reads (seed 0). The reference for each locus was the majority consensus of its first *Aicda*^{−/−} library, built with minimap2 and SAMtools consensus and iterated to convergence. The two off-targets of the same BioProject were added later and analyzed the same way, at 2,000 reads, with references built by the same consensus procedure (1,008 and 982 bp, converged in two iterations). Other loci of that BioProject were set aside: *Cd83* and *Ly6e* yielded no calls in any library, including at 30,000 reads, and the remaining cell contexts provide two libraries per group or a single *Aicda*^{−/−} library, which is below what the control-based test and the animal-level comparison need.

Two somatic callers that compare a case library with a matched normal, ClairS 0.5.1[@zheng2026] and DeepSomatic 1.9.0[@park2026], and two germline callers, Clair3 2.0.3[@zheng2022] and DeepVariant 1.9.0[@poplin2018], were run from their official Docker images on the same planted mutations, using the same alignments as LoFreq and restricted to the analysis window. For the somatic callers, the normal was the pooled usable reads of the other two AID-null libraries, the libraries from which SHMtrace's null is fitted. Each caller was run at its defaults for R10.4.1 nanopore reads (ClairS `ont_r10_dorado_sup_5khz`; Clair3 `r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v520`; DeepVariant `ONT_R104`; DeepSomatic `ONT`) and at the lowest allele fraction it accepts (ClairS `--snv_min_af 0.005 --min_coverage 4`; Clair3 `--snp_min_af 0.01 --min_coverage 4`; DeepVariant and DeepSomatic candidate thresholds of 1% and 0.5% of reads, with two supporting reads). PRJNA1481264 reports PromethION sequencing without the chemistry, so the same R10.4.1 models were used for Sμ and *Pim1*; those models assume a flow-cell and basecaller combination those libraries may not match, and a mismatch would count against the caller for reasons unrelated to SHM. This qualifies the somatic and germline callers on the public reads as LoFreq's design qualifies it on nanopore reads: comparators run outside the conditions they were built for, not evidence of general superiority either way. Substitutions with FILTER PASS below 0.5 allele fraction were kept, as for the other callers. To find the allele fraction at which the somatic callers begin to work, 30 substitutions were also planted into 25, 50, and 100 of 500 reads (5%, 10%, and 20%) of each held-out J_{H}4 control, which otherwise carries few mutations. ClairS and DeepSomatic were also run on the real AID-active libraries: the wild-type J_{H}4 libraries against the pooled *Aicda*^{−/−} reads, and the pMX-*Aicda* N114 V_{H} subclones against the pooled empty-vector reads (500 reads each, seed 0).

On real J_{H}4 libraries, ClairS reported one mutation and DeepSomatic at most 13, compared with 221, 344 and 73 SHMtrace calls; N114 totals were one, at most 14, and 70, 49 and 173, respectively. ClairS rejected both Wt3 candidates supported by ≥20% of reads. Among 1,197 retained calls, 53% were in <1%, 93% in <5% and 99.5% in <20% of reads. These results describe the tested settings and datasets rather than universal caller limits.

Figure 4's unique-density separation ranged 16–62-fold for Geneious and 2–40-fold across LoFreq settings. J_{H}4 Wt calls were 221, 344 and 73 versus 0, 2 and 0 in nulls; Geneious gave 203, 337 and 73 versus 2, 6 and 5. Default LoFreq gave 0, 11 and 0; BAQ-off gave 22 in Wt2. External Sμ Wt counts were 65–157 for SHMtrace and 52–131 for Geneious, with 0–2 versus 2–10 per null. The displayed Wt/null raster libraries had 34/35 other Q≥20 mismatches after germline exclusion; Wt added 5,643 mismatches at called sites. These are individual mismatch observations, distinct from unique variant counts.
Across the four planted datasets, permissive DeepSomatic produced at most 0.4 false calls per library under the evaluated settings.

Lineage simulations partitioned one null library into approximately forty power-law-sized clones. Each received a random 20-bp junction, J trimming from −3 to +12 bp, and S5F-weighted trunk, branch, subbranch and private mutations with gamma-distributed loads. In the expanded-clone scenario, one unmutated clone supplied 60% of reads. Each control was held out against the other two. Quantification was assessed at 125, 250, 500 and 1,000 reads on JH4/N114 V_{H} (168 libraries). Group simulations used log-normal animal rates (coefficient of variation 1), negative-binomial counts and 262,913 base observations per animal, across 300 experiments per condition. This represents approximately 526 covered bases per read at 500 reads, rather than complete coverage of the 529-bp window; observed per-read coverage ranged from 516 to 528 bases. Forty Sanger projects included realistic trace qualities, unusable traces and one of each planted tracking error. Junction clustering recovered clone assignments with adjusted Rand indices[@hubert1985] of 0.94–0.98.

PRJNA973112 (J_{H}4, positions 53–122, 5,000 merged read pairs per mouse), PRJNA918596 (CH12F3 VDJ, positions 21–249, 5,000 reads per replicate), and PRJNA820976 (Ramos VDJ, positions 26–446, 20,000 reads per clone, with indel calling) were analyzed with the same analysis engine and Illumina settings, using the AID-null groups as controls and the S5F model. PRJNA170048 (mOrange reporter, positions 75–693 of the study's own numbering, which is positions 31–649 of the 679-bp reference rebuilt here: that reference begins at position 45 of the study's numbering, so the two differ by a constant offset of 44. 200,000 of the first 600,000 reads per library, about 10,600 reads per position) was analyzed the same way, with the catalytically dead AID-E58Q-ER libraries of the empty-vector arm as controls and the dead-AID libraries of the other two arms left as samples; its reference was rebuilt from the position and reference-nucleotide columns of the study's own supplementary table, and the same table's per-position counts were used for the comparison with every-mismatch counting. The CH12F3 and Ramos references were the majority consensus of the control reads. Because these libraries are sequenced far beyond one read per molecule, mutation frequency rather than unique-variant density was compared. Read pairs were merged on an overlap of at least 20 bp with at most 10% mismatches (Figure S22). The PRJNA973112 and PRJNA918596 files as distributed carry a flat Q30 on every base; merging then writes Q60 where both mates agree, so the error model sees two levels whose value records whether both mates covered the base rather than how accurate the basecall is. Measured on the merged reads, PRJNA973112 is 93% Q60 and its 70-bp window lies inside the mate overlap, while PRJNA918596 is 88% Q30. Because quality carries no accuracy information in either, the single-read estimate reports the number of quality levels and flags both of these sets (`quality_levels`, `quality_flat`), and their single-read and combined densities are not interpretable. PRJNA820976 keeps binned qualities. UMI consensus was evaluated on 4,259 R10 reads of rRNA operons carrying 18-nt UMIs at both ends[@karst2021]. Reads were grouped by UMI (allowing up to three edits per end, with directional merging of rare UMIs), and each group of three or more reads was collapsed into one quality-weighted consensus, which was scored against the 43 known operon sequences of the mock community. On these dual-UMI R10 rRNA-operon reads[@karst2021], consensus reduced error 46-fold (95% CI 30–83) to 0.21%, with residual errors concentrated in homopolymer indels; at ≥10 reads per family, substitution error approached one per 10,000 bases (Figure S9H). This is a technical consensus benchmark rather than an SHM experiment.

The noisy null library carried 36 substitutions, 61% at G:C, while the other two had none. Retaining it as a decoy suppressed all sample substitution calls. Excluding it from decoys, while retaining it in model fitting, yielded 86–97% G:C calls; treating it as a sample instead yielded 71–84%. The rule was developed from this dataset, so this is a sensitivity analysis rather than independent validation of that rule.

The source study's Q>20 every-mismatch counts gave inactive-AID background of 0.31–0.72 per 10^{3} bases, approximately two-fold active/inactive separation in the empty arm, and 43–66% G:C transitions in inactive backgrounds. SHMtrace's inactive Ugi and UNG arms retained 0 and 2 calls, respectively. Calling across contexts used inactive-AID empty-arm controls. The paired effect and interval use one transition-share value per experiment; the pooled 95%/4% shares have a different weighting and need not subtract to the paired mean difference.

PRJNA831666[@vincendeau2022] holds Sμ–Sγ1 switch products from wild-type, *Shld1*^{−/−}, *Xlf*^{−/−} and *Shld1*^{−/−}*Xlf*^{−/−} primary B cells, three mice per genotype, one PacBio run per mouse. Although the archive names the files as subreads, the reads are of high-accuracy quality: aligned to the bundled Sμ fragment over 600 bp or more, their median identity is 99.8%, so the `map-hifi` preset was used in place of the module's `map-ont` default. Donor and acceptor references were cut from the GRCm39 IgH locus (chromosome 12, minus-strand orientation): Sμ with the forward primer site, chr12:113,386,000–113,392,500, and Sγ1 through Cγ1 to the reverse primer site, chr12:113,290,000–113,304,000, the windows being fixed by where the reads themselves start and stop (`crm/build_switch_reference.py`, which refuses to write unless the project's own J_{H}4 reference and the bundled Sμ fragment both align inside the fetched locus). Junctions were called with `shmtrace.switch` (`crm/switch_pacbio.py`): reads were oriented to the donor, the donor and acceptor parts taken as the two best forward alignments, and junctions whose breakpoints agreed within 3 bp on both sides counted once as a unique junction. Each library also carries a large population of short off-target molecules, median about 350 bp against about 1.3 kb for the reads that yield junctions, so read accounting is reported per sample. Genotypes were compared with one value per mouse, by Welch test and by permutation; with three mice per genotype the permutation p cannot fall below 0.1, so both are reported. The fifteen comparisons there, five features against three genotypes, are reported unadjusted, with each group mean beside its p value so the size of the difference is visible and not only its significance. Adjusting them together by Benjamini–Hochberg changes nothing: nine reach 0.05 before and nine after. The engineered-diversification contrast of Figure S19A is a single pre-specified comparison, AID against APOBEC3A in each genotype, so no adjustment arises there. Acceptor-breakpoint ambiguity was measured directly, by re-aligning each junction's first 60 acceptor bases on their own with the short-read preset and counting placements within five matched bases of the best, because the module's own flag depends on secondary alignments that minimap2 does not report for these reads. What that ambiguity costs the comparisons was then measured rather than assumed (`crm/switch_ambiguity_sensitivity.py`): dropping every junction whose acceptor segment has more than one near-equal placement removes 2–21% of a sample's junctions, and 13 of the 15 genotype comparisons stay on the same side of 0.05. Two do not, in opposite directions: microhomology of four bases or more in *Shld1*^{−/−} strengthens from p = 0.065 to 0.005, and insertions in *Xlf*^{−/−} weaken from p = 0.016 to 0.060. Those two should be read as provisional. Because reads per unique junction vary between samples, counts reflect PCR recovery rather than switching efficiency, and 19–47% of unique junctions place equally well at more than one acceptor position.

Mean-microhomology comparisons against Wt gave p=0.92 for *Shld1*, 0.0092 for *Xlf* and 9.3 × 10^{−5} for the double mutant. The ≥4-nt share rose from 7% to 18% (p=0.0053), and blunt junctions fell from 21% to 7% (p=0.0028). *Shld1* insertion-bearing junctions were 48% versus 31% in Wt (p=0.0074). Reads per unique junction ranged 1.1–23.3; inferred structures do not measure switching efficiency.

Two datasets in which a deaminase is directed deliberately were analysed against the construct each experiment began with, which is what `ancestral_reference` is for: there the reference is a known ancestor, so a change that selection drove high is the result and not germline. The option is off by default and leaves the physiological presets unchanged (`crm/germline_policy_demo.py` shows what it does and does not alter). SRP159221[@liu2018] edits one 238-bp EGFP amplicon with a panel of editors delivered alike, three replicates per arm; pairs merge on a 97.8% overlap, the reference is the consensus of the no-editor arm, and the prespecified contrast was DBE-AIDmono against DBE-humanA3a in wild-type and UNG/MSH2-null 293T, at 20,000 reads per library (`crm/liu_mutators.py`). Motif and spectrum shares are descriptive: they are computed from whatever was called and never used to decide what to call. The anti-HLA-A2 clones[@devilder2019] were taken from the study's Additional file 1, which publishes each selected cluster's nucleotide sequence together with the authors' own list of its mutations; each cluster is kept separate and nothing is collapsed to a consensus (`crm/devilder_clones.py`). Comparing the two lists position by position, SHMtrace recovers **every one of the 150 mutations the authors report across the 42 selected clusters, and calls nothing they do not report**: 17 clusters and 31 mutations in the first round, 25 clusters and 119 in the second, with no cluster differing in either direction. That is the sharpest available test of variant identity on this route, because the comparator is an independently curated list rather than another run of the same software. The Devilder records are selected cluster sequences, not a sampled population, so they are used to compare variant identities and no population frequency, unselected distribution or technical error rate is computed from them.

GSE77788[@compagno2017] comprises Sμ libraries from Wt/Aicda−/− primary B cells under DMSO, idelalisib or duvelisib, three replicates per genotype/treatment. All nine null libraries are paired, whereas six Wt libraries are 300-bp single-end. Against the bundled 651-bp reference, R1 covers 401–650, single reads 351–650 and R2 1–250. Most pairs do not overlap; merging retains only 9–21%, preferentially short products. Analyses therefore use R1 alone or the single-end file over shared positions 410–625, excluding primer/end sequence. Each treatment is analyzed separately against its own null controls at 20,000 reads per library. The repeat interval, positions 1–327, is reached by R2; a second analysis uses positions 20–240 in the twelve paired libraries. Its three Wt libraries represent one per treatment, so the pooled genotype contrast is descriptive rather than a balanced treatment-adjusted design (`crm/public_smu_pi3k.py`).

Groups were compared with one value per library, each library being one animal, subclone, clone, culture or experiment as Table S2 states; reads were never treated as replicates. The Welch test on log_{10} rates is the primary test throughout, chosen before the analyses reported here; the negative-binomial and permutation tests are reported alongside it as sensitivity analyses, and Figure S9E compares all three. The negative-binomial test models each library's mutation count k with mean n·r, where n is that library's bases and r its group's rate, and variance n·r + φ(n·r)^{2} with one dispersion φ shared by both groups and fitted by maximum likelihood under the full model. No moderation or shrinkage across features is applied, since there is one endpoint. The statistic is the likelihood ratio against a common rate, and its null distribution comes from 499 parametric bootstrap samples drawn under that common rate with the fitted φ, because two to ten libraries per group are too few for the asymptotic χ^{2}. A group with no calls keeps rate zero rather than being floored. The permutation test is exact when the number of allocations allows, which sets a floor on the p value it can return: with three libraries per group there are only 20 allocations, so the smallest two-sided p is 0.10 and the test cannot reach 0.05 whatever the difference. Its apparent power of zero at n = 3 in Figure S9E is therefore arithmetic, not a property of the data, and it is why the Welch test is primary at these group sizes. Each cell of Figure S9E is 300 simulated experiments, so a reported share carries a Monte Carlo 95% interval no wider than ±5.6 percentage points (Wilson); under the null at n = 3 the Welch test rejected in 3.7% (95% CI 2.1–6.4) and the negative-binomial test in 5.0% (3.1–8.1), while pooling reads rejected in 91.3% (87.6–94.0). The Welch test uses log_{10} rates, with libraries without calls placed at their one-event density; a fold against such libraries therefore depends on that convention and is not a confidence bound. The same rule, one event on the library's own exposure, is used for every log-scale test, fold and plotted geometric mean; the software also reports each test with half an event and with a third of the smallest observed rate, as labelled sensitivity analyses, never as the primary result. The permutation test is exact. Folds are ratios of geometric means. Spectra were compared by pooled Pearson correlation across the 12 substitution types with a Fisher interval, by a repeated-measures test of the platform-by-substitution-type interaction with mouse as the matching factor, and by paired Šídák-adjusted t tests. Sample sizes, statistical tests, and dispersion measures are given in each figure legend. Analyses used Python 3.13 with NumPy and SciPy[@virtanen2020]. For the two CH12 off-target loci, Welch tests on mutation frequency gave p = 0.024 (off-target 1) and 0.030 (off-target 2).
